Stage 1 · Warm-up

Agree to disagree

Disagreeing well is a skill. Disagreeing badly ends the conversation and changes nobody’s mind.

💬⚡

BEmployers are prohibited from sending email to staff after six.
CCars over ten years old are banned from the city centre.
DAnybody who returns lost property receives a reward paid by the state.

3 · Read the claim. How far do you agree?
A claim

“Nobody has ever been argued out of a position by somebody who told them they were wrong. People move when they are given a reason that fits what they already believe — and when the other side has clearly understood them first.”

Take a position and defend it in pairs. Your partner must try to move you using the method in the claim.Take a position and defend it. 1 · Read the explanation.
Two systems, one argument

Everything in this stage has already been taught. Lesson 5 gave you the obligation system — must, have to, mustn’t, don’t have to, can, should. Lesson 6 gave you the deduction system — must have, can’t have, might have. In an argument both are working at once, and the difference between a strong speaker and a weak one is usually which system they reach for.

Arguing about a rule needs the obligation system, and it needs one extra step: should have to. People should pay more is advice to drivers. People should have to pay more is an argument about what the law ought to require. Only the second one is a position on the policy.

Three moves worth stealing
  • Concede, then object. You may well be right about the cost, but the same service should still cost the same. The concession costs nothing and makes the objection much harder to dismiss.
  • Remove the obligation your opponent assumed. Nobody has to buy a new car to benefit — hybrids get a fifth off. Half of all disagreements are about a duty that does not exist.
  • Reject the claim, not the person. That can’t be the whole story attacks the argument. You can’t be serious attacks the speaker, and nobody has ever changed their mind after hearing it.
2 · Study the examples.
Job in the argumentExample

what the rule should be, formalDrivers ought to be required to declare emissions.
the rule as it standsOlder cars have to pay the higher rate from April.
a written regulationAll vehicles must display a valid permit.
what should be forbiddenEmployers shouldn’t be allowed to email staff at midnight.
what is forbidden nowEmployers are prohibited from contacting staff after six.
removing an obligationDrivers don’t have to buy a new car to benefit.
removing an obligation, formalResidents needn’t apply again this year.
a real limitI can’t afford to replace it.
rejecting a present claimThat can’t be the whole story.

rejecting a past claimThey can’t have read the report before voting.

Two things to watch

1 — Should and should have to are different positions. People should drive less tells individuals what to do. People should have to pay more tells the legislature what to require. Mixing them up is why some arguments never meet.

2 — Can’t is doing three jobs. Inability (I can’t afford it), prohibition (You can’t park here) and deduction (That can’t be right). Only the context separates them, and in an argument all three appear within a minute of each other.

Reporting a rule and proposing one are different jobs

In an argument the modal tells the reader whether you are describing the world or trying to change it. Older cars have to pay the higher rate reports what is already the case. Everyone should have to pay the same proposes a rule that does not yet exist — and the double modal is not a mistake: should carries your opinion, have to carries the obligation you want created. The formal equivalent is ought to be required to.

The same split runs through prohibition. Employers are prohibited from contacting staff after six reports a regulation; Employers shouldn’t be allowed to email at midnight demands one. Keep don’t have to out of that argument entirely: it removes an obligation and forbids nothing, which is why Drivers don’t have to buy a new car to benefit works as a reassurance, never as a ban.

Attacking a claim, and conceding one

Modals of deduction do the work of disagreement without calling anybody a liar. About the present: That can’t be the whole story rejects; There must be a reason nobody has mentioned asserts. About the past, add have + past participle: They can’t have read the report before voting · Somebody must have seen the figures. This is the polite register of argument in English: the claim is attacked, not the person.

Conceding is a modal move too. You may well be right about the cost gives ground without surrendering the argument, and it is normally followed by a turn: That might be true in the city, but not in the villages. Softening works the same way — I’m not sure that can be the whole story is the same rejection with the edge taken off, and in writing it is usually the stronger move.

Errors to watch: Everyone should to have to pay → should have to pay · They mustn’t have read it (as a rejection) → can’t have read it · Employers don’t have to email at midnight when you mean a ban → shouldn’t be allowed to · You may well right → you may well be right.

5 · Read the model letter.
Model

Sir,

I am writing to support the council’s proposal to link parking charges to vehicle emissions, and to answer the objection raised in your pages last week.

That objection may well be right about who pays. The oldest cars do tend to belong to the people with the least money, and a charge that falls hardest on them would be difficult to defend. But it is not the charge the council has proposed. Nobody has to buy a new car to benefit: hybrids pay a fifth less from the first day, and residents on the lowest incomes are exempt altogether.

The stronger argument is the one nobody has made. A charge of this kind is an incentive rather than a punishment, and it is the only measure available to us that requires no new public spending at a time when the legislature is cutting it everywhere else.

If the scheme goes ahead, the revenue should have to be spent on buses and on nothing else. I would urge readers to say so before the vote on the fourteenth.

Yours faithfully,
